docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
This wiki is the reference guide for data developers who produce and maintain the base year model inputs for the SEMCOG UrbanSim land use simulation. It documents every required data table, organized by data domain — the logical subject area the data belongs to.

Each domain page describes the expected structure, column definitions, and quality requirements for that domain's data. The final assembly step — combining all inputs into the model input file — is handled by a separate procedure.

Base year: The base year changes with each forecast cycle. Where this wiki refers to the "base year," substitute the actual base year for the cycle you are working on.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Term Meaning UrbanSim Agent-based land use simulation model that forecasts household, employment, and building changes year by year Base year The starting year of the simulation. All input tables represent conditions as of this year. The base year is 2020 for the RDF2050 forecast and is expected to be 2024 or 2025 for the RDF2055 forecast HDF5 / HDF A binary data file format used to store all model input tables in one file. Can be opened and inspected with pandas.HDFStore in Python or the free HDFView application HLCM Household Location Choice Model — statistical model that determines where simulated households choose to live each year ELCM Employment Location Choice Model — statistical model that determines where simulated jobs locate each year TAZ Traffic Analysis Zone — the unit of geography used by the travel demand model; parcels are assigned to TAZs MCD Minor Civil Division — cities, townships, and villages. The official geographic unit for municipal-level control SEMMCD / semmcd SEMCOG's internal MCD identifier. This is the primary geography code used throughout the model city_id A column that appears in many tables. Outside the City of Detroit, city_id equals semmcd and refers to a municipality. Inside the City of Detroit, city_id is a neighborhood identifier, not a municipal code. This is a legacy naming choice — treat city_id as "semmcd or Detroit neighborhood id" depending on context large_area One of 8 modeling zones used for forecast segmentation and control totals. Corresponds to Michigan counties by FIPS code, except Wayne County is split into two zones: City of Detroit (code 5) and Wayne County excluding Detroit (code 3) REMI Regional Economic Models, Inc. — the economic forecasting model that produces the population and employment projections used as control totals PopulationSim Open-source population synthesis tool that generates a synthetic base-year population of households and persons matching census distributions Pandana Python library used to compute network-based accessibility indicators (walk/bike/drive travel times and cumulative destination counts) Proforma The developer model's financial feasibility analysis — estimates construction cost vs. expected revenue to determine whether new buildings are profitable to build

docs.title: Data Dependency Chain
docs.text:
The most important structural rule in the model is: every agent (household or job) must be in a building, and every building must be in a parcel. This three-level chain is the spatial backbone of the simulation. Referential integrity breaks anywhere in this chain will cause model errors.

flowchart TD
    R[SEMCOG Region] --> CO[7 Counties]
    CO --> LA["8 Large Areas<br/>(Wayne split into Detroit + suburbs)"]
    LA --> MCD[238 MCDs]
    LA --> TAZ[2,811 TAZs]
    TAZ --> MAZ["~28,647 MAZs<br/>(micro_zones — anchor geography)"]

    MCD --> P["~2M Parcels"]
    MAZ --> P

    P --> B["~1.8M Buildings"]
    MAZ --> B
    B --> HH[Households]
    B --> J[Jobs]

    style HH fill:#00897B,color:#fff
    style J  fill:#1E88E5,color:#fff
    style B  fill:#43A047,color:#fff
    style P  fill:#43A047,color:#fff
    style LA fill:#e0f2f1,stroke:#00897B
    style MAZ fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#e65100

MAZ (micro_zones) is the anchor spatial unit for parcels and buildings. Each parcel carries both a maz_id and a zone_id (TAZ) column. The two are kept consistent through the 1:1 MAZ→TAZ crosswalk — the parcel's TAZ matches its MAZ's parent zone rather than being assigned independently.

Buildings also carry their own maz_id. It is initialized from the parcel maz_id, except where building_to_maz_override supplies a building-specific MAZ. A building zone_id (TAZ) is always derived from that building MAZ through the micro_zones crosswalk, not independently assigned from its parcel.

Real-world alignment note

The hierarchy above is the intended clean structure. In practice, real-world data introduces boundary complications that data developers should keep in mind:

  • TAZ–parcel boundary mismatch — TAZ boundaries are designed for travel modeling and do not always align with parcel boundaries. A parcel that physically straddles two TAZ zones is assigned to one TAZ based on its centroid location.
  • MAZ/TAZ–building override — because MAZ is the anchor unit, a building on a parcel that straddles a MAZ (and therefore TAZ) boundary can be assigned its own maz_id/zone_id by building location via the building_to_maz_override table, overriding the parcel-inherited value.
  • MCD–parcel boundary mismatch — A small number of parcels may physically cross a municipal boundary. These are assigned to the MCD containing their centroid, which may not reflect the parcel's full extent.
  • Multi-parcel buildings — A single building can span multiple parcels (large campuses, industrial complexes). These are tracked separately in the multi_parcel_buildings table.

These edge cases are small in number but can affect spatial aggregation and model outputs. Follow the centroid-based assignment scheme as the standard approach. When exceptions or unusual cases are encountered during data preparation, document them with a note so the modeling team can assess the impact and develop targeted solutions if needed.

docs.title: How Inputs Are Assembled
docs.text:
Data from all domains is collected and assembled into a single model input file by a separate data assembly procedure. That procedure draws from four source types:

  • PostgreSQL — parcels, buildings, zoning, events, demolitions, crime rates
  • CSV / Excel files — control totals, rate tables, synthetic population, jobs, amenities
  • Prior / Reference HDF — stable tables that do not change between forecast cycles and are carried forward from a previous model input file. Includes: counties, large_areas, employment_sectors
  • Network HDF (semcog_networks.h5) — street network geometry used directly by the simulation at runtime; not included in the model input file

Each domain's data developer is responsible for producing their data to the specifications in this wiki. The assembly and final validation steps are handled outside individual domain procedures.

docs.title: Output Files
docs.text:
The data preparation pipeline delivers three HDF files to the simulation. All three must be present at simulation startup.

File Role Contents forecast_data_input.h5 Main simulation database — the primary output of the data assembly pipeline All base-year agent and geography tables (households, buildings, parcels, jobs, persons, zones, etc.) plus supplemental reference tables: income_growth_rates, remi_pce_growth_rate, taz_demographic_snapshots, acs_household_change_by_block_group, points_of_interest_by_category. See domain pages for the full table list and Table Catalog for a complete index. semcog_networks.h5 Pandana street network bundle — produced by a separate network build step; not assembled from domain data osm_walk_2024, osm_bike_2024, osm_bike_comfort_2024, highway_ext_2020 (+ _local). Used by the simulation each year to recompute dynamic neighborhood accessibility as households and jobs shift. Only walk and highway are built at runtime. The 2030 highway network and the retired osm_roads_walk_2020 were dropped Jul 2026 — see Street Networks. access_indicators.h5 Pre-computed accessibility indicators — produced by the Pandana accessibility pipeline; regenerated when the network, POI, or transit data is refreshed Walk, bike, bike-comfort, drive and transit metrics by parcel (travel times to destinations + cumulative job counts within thresholds). All five tables share one parcel index. Held constant throughout the run; the simulation reads only walk, bike and drive. Written compressed (blosc:zstd) — 348 MB vs 2,196 MB raw.

Filename note: These names are stable conventions — they do not encode dates, vintages, or forecast horizons. Version control and provenance are tracked in the data development pipeline, not in the filename.

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text:
Primary sources: Pre-computed accessibility indicator CSVs; transit stop and POI datasets

Accessibility tables measure how easily each parcel can reach destinations by walking, biking, or driving. Transit stops and points of interest are the destination inputs that drive accessibility analysis; the indicator tables are the outputs used directly as model features.

docs.title: transit_stops
docs.text:
Fixed-route bus and rail stop locations used in accessibility computation and as HLCM/ELCM features.

Index: stop_id (unique)

Column Type Rules Notes stop_id object unique, no null Transit agency stop ID point_x float64 no null State plane X coordinate point_y float64 no null State plane Y coordinate

Only point_x and point_y are retained in the exported model input — any additional source columns are dropped.

Update: Get updated stop locations from SEMCOG transit database or GTFS feeds. Reproject to state plane if needed. Include all fixed-route bus and rail stops in the 7-county region.

Common issues: - Stops outside the region — verify coordinates - Duplicate stop_id values — append agency prefix to ensure uniqueness

docs.title: points_of_interest_by_category
docs.text:
Destination locations used in accessibility analysis, organized by facility type. Multiple distinct categories are present — each category drives a separate set of nearest-POI accessibility variables in the model. The categories currently in use are: grocery stores, hospitals, health centers, urgent care centers, libraries, parks (local, bike-accessible, and school), pharmacies, childcare, fire stations, American Job Centers, community colleges, passenger train stations, and passenger airports.

Note on orca table name: The simulation registers this table internally as poi (the orca table name). The HDF storage key is points_of_interest_by_category. Code referencing the orca table uses poi; the HDF key is what appears in the data file.

Index: Row index (integer)

Column Type Rules Notes category object no null Facility type label (e.g., "grocery_store", "hospital", "park_local") — must match the destination names used in the accessibility analysis configuration point_x float64 no null State plane X coordinate point_y float64 no null State plane Y coordinate

Update: Refresh from the latest accessibility analysis POI dataset. Any change to category names or the set of categories requires a full re-run of the accessibility analysis — the indicator variable names in the model's accessibility configuration are derived from these category labels, and a mismatch causes errors at simulation startup. Coordinate with the accessibility analysis team before making category changes.

Common issues: - Category name mismatch between this table and the accessibility analysis configuration — causes missing or misnamed indicator variables - POIs outside the 7-county region — verify coordinates before use

docs.title: Accessibility Indicator Tables
docs.text:
All indicator tables share the same structure — indexed by parcel_id, with one row per parcel, and all tables carry the identical parcel index so they can be joined without reindexing. They contain two variable types:

Near-max variables — travel time to the nearest facility. Lower = better access. Fill value when no route exists is the mode's max_distance, which is not the number in the column name (the name carries the search horizon, the fill carries the top-code):

Mode Column suffix Fill when unreachable Walk _near_max90 95 Bike / bike comfort _near_max120 125 Transit _near_max120 125 Drive _near_max150 155

Cumulative and gravity variables — count (or weighted sum) of jobs or transit stops reachable within a threshold. Higher = better access. Fill value when none reachable: 0.

Indicator CSVs are date-stamped per mode (e.g. walk_indicators_by_parcel_20260722.csv) and combined into a single HDF by forecast_data_input/accessibility/build_access_indicators_hdf.py.

Compression matters here. The combined HDF is written with format="fixed", complevel=5, complib="blosc:zstd" — 2,196 MB uncompressed vs 348 MB compressed, values identical. Compression must be applied at write time: pandas' format="fixed" without complevel writes plain PyTables Array nodes, which cannot be compressed afterwards, so ptrepack is a no-op on them.

docs.title: accessibility_bike_comfort_indicator_by_parcel
docs.text:
Index: parcel_id

Same destination and threshold set as the bike table, but computed on the bicycle level-of-traffic-stress network rather than the plain bike network. Variable names follow {destination}_bike_comfort_near_max120.

The stress network's edge costs (minutes_w1, minutes_w2) are both penalised — neither is real travel time. Against the unpenalised bike network, 86.1% of edges are unpenalised in both, but 11.1% of w1 and 12.0% of w2 edges exceed 1.5x (overall 1.110x and 1.155x). The accessibility pipeline routes on minutes_w2. Consequently times in this table are stress-weighted minutes, not clock minutes, and are not directly comparable with the plain bike table.

docs.title: accessibility_transit_indicator_by_parcel
docs.text:
Index: parcel_id

Peak/off-peak transit access, computed from the pandana transit networks. Pattern {destination}_transit_near_max120, plus jobs_transit_cumulative_{15,20,30,45,60,90}min and jobs_transit_gravity_90min.

Roughly 47.5% of parcels are within the transit service area; the rest are filled as unreachable (125 min / 0 jobs). That is a real coverage boundary, not missing data.

The simulation does not use this table. Model transit measures come from travel_data.am_transit_total_time (TAZ-to-TAZ skims from the travel model), a different source — see variables_tract.py.

docs.title: How Indicators Join to Buildings
docs.text: All tables are indexed by parcel_id. The simulation joins them to buildings via buildings.parcel_id. This join is handled automatically during model variable computation.

docs.title: Which Indicators Go Stale During a Forecast
docs.text:
Not everything in these tables ages the same way, and the distinction is by what the indicator depends on, not by mode:

Class Changes during a run? Handling *_near_max* (POI-nearest) No — POIs and networks are fixed for the run Correctly held constant; refresh per forecast vintage jobs_*_cumulative_*, jobs_*_gravity_* Yes — job locations move every simulated year Held constant; a known approximation Neighborhood variables (nodes_walk, nodes_drv) Yes Already recomputed every year by the neighborhood_vars step

The frozen jobs_* measures are the only place holding values constant introduces real error. The exposure is limited because the model also computes fresh annual job access from networks_drv.yaml (log_sum_{15,30,45,60}min_jobs) — but that redundancy is a trap: a spec author can pick the frozen variable without realising it never updates.

Nothing needs recomputing mid-run. Recompute the whole bundle when POIs, networks, or the base-year jobs/parcels change — i.e. per forecast vintage.

docs.title: Network Bundle
docs.text:
The pandana networks the simulation rebuilds each year are documented separately — see Street Networks. Relevant points for accessibility work:

  • The accessibility pipeline and the simulation now share the same drive network (highway_ext_2020, from highway_ext_2020_UPDATED.shp).
  • They still use different walk networks: the simulation uses osm_walk_2024 (936,001 nodes / 1,380,659 edges) from semcog_networks.h5, while the accessibility run reads network_walkbike_2024_aug2025.h5 directly. Same source build, but do not assume node IDs correspond.
  • The transit networks (network_transit_{peak,offpeak}_aug2025.h5, ~1.5 GB each) are used only by the accessibility pipeline. The simulation declares no transit network.

docs.title: Update Procedure
docs.text:
Accessibility indicators should be regenerated when: - The street or transit network changes significantly - The POI or transit stop dataset is refreshed - A new forecast cycle requires updated base-year accessibility

Steps: 1. Update points_of_interest_by_category and transit_stops with current data 2. Run the accessibility analysis (Pandana-based pipeline) 3. Export new indicator CSVs with a date stamp in the filename 4. Update the relevant file path references in the model configuration 5. Re-assemble the model input file to incorporate the new indicators 6. If variable names or columns changed, coordinate with the modeling team — model coefficients are estimated on specific variable names; renaming requires re-estimation

Common issues: - Parcels with all values at fill value (95/125/155 min) — parcel has no network connection; check coordinates - Column name mismatch between CSV and model configuration — causes errors at simulation startup - parcel_id values in indicator CSVs that don't match the current parcels table — verify the accessibility analysis used the same parcel dataset

docs.title: households
docs.text:
Base-year synthetic household table. Generated by PopulationSim and placed into buildings using a stable-marriage matching algorithm that aligns synthesized households to building assessor records at the block group level. Matching is based on shared attributes including building type, number of units, market value / housing cost, year built, and tenure.

Index: household_id (unique)

Column Type Rules Notes household_id int32 unique, no null building_id int32 join → buildings, no null Placement result; -1 = unplaced persons int8 range [1–20], no null Household size workers int8 range [0–18], no null Employed workers age_of_head int8 range [15–100], no null Age of head income float64 no null Annual income ($); negatives set to 0 children int8 range [0–14], no null Children under 18 cars int8 values: 0–6 Vehicle count race_id int8 values: 1,2,3,4 1=White, 2=Black, 3=Asian, 4=Other

docs.title: How the model uses key household columns
docs.text: Column Used by (model step) How it's used / why it matters building_id (-1 = unplaced) HLCM -1 flags a household the HLCM must place this year. Each year households_relocation un-places a share (sets -1) so they re-choose; new households from households_transition also start at -1. children, income (+ household senior count, from person ages) HLCM segmentation The HLCM is split into segments by children (has / none), income (low / mid / high), and seniors (with / without), per large area. has_children comes from children > 0; the income tier from income; the senior flag from whether any household member is a senior (person ages). Household size (persons) and age_of_head are not HLCM segmentation dimensions. workers workers_adjustment_model (formerly fix_lpr) After each transition, this step swaps a household for a seed household with one more / fewer worker so the employed-worker count matches the employed_workers_rate targets by large area and age band; income and cars are then resampled to match. age_of_head, persons, children, income, cars, workers, race_id control totals / households_transition These are the demographic bracket dimensions in annual_household_control_totals; the transition step adds or removes households to hit the target counts per bracket. large_area_id (via the building) HLCM, control totals Determines which per-large-area HLCM applies and which control-total rows the household counts toward.

docs.title: taz_demographic_snapshots
docs.text:
TAZ-level demographic counts for historical reference years. Used to compute neighborhood change trend features in the HLCM — specifically, the 5-year and 10-year change in household counts, population, jobs, housing units, and household composition by TAZ.

The simulation tracks these counts annually in memory (the taz_hlcm_trend_by_year injectable), building up a record year by year as it runs forward. This table seeds that record for years before the simulation starts, making historical change visible at the start of the forecast.

Index: Composite — taz_id × snapshot_year

Column Type Notes snapshot_year int16 Historical reference year (e.g., 2010, 2015) taz_id int32 Traffic analysis zone ID hh_count int32 Number of households hh_pop int32 Household population hu_count int32 Housing units nonres_sqft int32 Non-residential square footage job_count int32 Jobs with_children int32 Households with children with_senior int32 Households with seniors one_person_hh int32 Single-person households

Currently included years: 2010 (seeds the 10-year lookback) and 2015 (seeds the 5-year lookback). Source: 2010 data extracted from base tables in model_improvements/2024_spring/2010_data/; 2015 data extracted from the 2045 forecast HDF.

Extend when needed: The available snapshot_year values determine which trend lags the HLCM can use. As the forecast horizon extends (e.g., to 2055), the simulation builds up its own annual record, so no additional historical rows are required for the forecast itself. Add earlier snapshots (e.g., 2005) only if longer lookback windows are introduced.

docs.title: acs_household_change_by_block_group
docs.text:
Block group occupied housing unit counts from two ACS survey vintages. Used by the mcd_hu_sampling step to distribute city-level household growth sub-city: block groups where occupancy has been growing attract proportionally more new households; block groups where occupancy has been declining attract fewer.

Index: block_group_geoid (Census block group GEOID, integer — leading zeros removed)

Column Type Notes block_group_geoid int64 Census block group GEOID — unique index occupied_hu_current int32 Occupied housing units, more recent ACS vintage occupied_hu_prior int32 Occupied housing units, earlier ACS vintage

The model computes occupied_hu_current − occupied_hu_prior as the trend signal. Column names are vintage-neutral — when updating, replace the values in both columns and record the survey years in the update notes. Current vintage: 2019 (current) and 2014 (prior), ACS 5-year estimates.

Update: When starting a new forecast cycle, pull occupied housing unit counts from ACS (5-year estimates) for all block groups in the 7-county region. Shift the old occupied_hu_current values into occupied_hu_prior, then populate occupied_hu_current with the new vintage. Document which ACS years are in use.

Common issues: - Missing block groups — all block groups in the model region must be present; gaps produce fill-rate anomalies in sampling - block_group_geoid must be stored as integer (leading zeros removed); verify dtype after loading - Block groups that were split or merged between ACS vintages must be resolved before use

docs.title: Development & Context
docs.text:
Primary sources: PostgreSQL event and demolition tables; CSV files; crime data from PostgreSQL; construction cost estimates; REMI price index forecasts

This domain brings together four related categories:

  • Planned development events — specific buildings that will be added or removed at known future years, plus background demolition rates
  • Neighborhood context — school quality and crime rates that influence location choice
  • Building construction costs — per-square-foot construction cost estimates by building type and area, which determine feasibility of new development
  • Price growth rates — REMI-derived annual PCE inflation applied to construction costs each simulation year (property-value appreciation is a separate, large-area-specific personal-income series documented under Demographics)

docs.title: Development Events
docs.text:
Key distinction between event tables:

  • events_addition / events_deletion are real estate events — they add or remove physical buildings in the simulation. Use these for known construction projects or planned demolitions where the structure itself is changing.
  • refiner_events is an agent-level event — it adds or removes jobs, households, or group quarters persons at targeted locations without changing the building inventory. Use this for planned employment relocations, major employer openings or closings, facility population changes, and other events that affect who occupies buildings rather than what buildings exist.

Event timing is by year, not date. Every event's timing is a single integer year — year_built on events_addition, year_demo on events_deletion (renamed to year_built on load), and the year column on refiner_events. There is no calendar date anywhere in the chain: the source tables carry only the year column, the input SQL pulls only that year column, and the model fires an event in the year whose value equals the current simulation year (year_built == iter_var in the scheduled add/demolish steps; refinements.year == year in the refiner).

What this means for developing event tables: all events sharing a year are applied together — there is no within-year ordering, sequencing, or partial-year timing. When curating event records, only the year matters; a month or day has no effect on when (or whether) an event fires. Assign each event to the year it should take effect and do not attempt to encode sub-year dates — they are neither stored nor read.

docs.title: Base-year event cutoff
docs.text:
The input build assembles buildings as the base-year snapshot from the preceding building GIS view plus the two physical-event tables. It first removes deletion events dated in the base year, then appends addition events dated in the base year. For the current cycle, the complete 2024 building view plus complete 2025 additions and deletions produces the 2025 buildings snapshot.

This gives a clear acceptance rule for the base inventory: it is complete when the preceding-year GIS building view is complete and every physical addition and deletion for the base year has been entered. Event records after the base year stay in their event tables. They can be added, corrected, or dropped without rebuilding the current base-year buildings snapshot; the forecast captures them when it reaches their year.

Do not also place a future event directly in buildings, because that would cause the physical change to be represented twice. Conversely, do not omit a base-year event from the assembly run, because the base snapshot would be stale.

docs.title: events_addition
docs.text:
Known physical building additions, such as planned developments, stadiums, and hospitals. A row dated in the base year is incorporated into the assembled buildings snapshot. A row dated after the base year remains a scheduled forecast input and adds a building when its year is reached.

Index: objectid (unique)

Column Type Rules Notes objectid int unique, no null Index parcel_id int32 no null Must exist in parcels building_type_id int8 join → building_types, no null year_built int16 base year or later, no null Year the building is added residential_units int16 no null 0 for non-residential non_residential_sqft int32 no null 0 for residential stories int — gqcap int ≥ 0, no null Facility group-quarters capacity; 0 means the event does not create a GQ facility event_id int unique, no null Stable event identifier. Retain it across input refreshes; refiner_events may use it to target the resulting event building. building_id int — Optional source-system building reference. It is not the identifier assigned to the event-created building in forecast outputs.

For an event that creates a GQ facility, set gqcap to the number of beds. Do not infer GQ capacity from building_type_id; use 0 when the event does not create a GQ facility.

Common issues: - parcel_id not in parcels — building can't be placed; fix parcel reference - a base-year row missing from the assembly run — the base buildings snapshot will be incomplete - year_built before the base year — verify the forecast-cycle cutoff and source record

docs.title: events_deletion
docs.text:
Known physical building deletions or demolitions. A row dated in the base year removes the building while the base snapshot is assembled. A row dated after the base year remains a scheduled forecast input and removes the building when its year is reached.

Index: objectid (unique)

Column Type Rules Notes objectid int unique, no null building_id int32 no null Building to be demolished year_built int16 base year or later, no null Year of demolition. The source field is year_demo; it is normalized to year_built in the model-input HDF.

Common issues: - building_id not in buildings — skipped but should be cleaned up - a base-year demolition missing from the assembly run — the base buildings snapshot will be stale - Demolition year before the base year — verify the forecast-cycle cutoff and source record

docs.title: refiner_events
docs.text:
Agent-level events collected from various sources. Unlike events_addition/events_deletion, this table does not change the building inventory — it adds or removes agents (jobs, households, or group quarters persons) at specific locations. Typical uses include planned major employer openings or relocations, GQ facility population changes, and other future occupancy events that do not involve new construction or demolition. Assembled by merging employment events and GQ events CSVs.

Index: refinement_id (unique, int16)

Column Type Rules Notes refinement_id int16 unique, no null transaction_id int16 no null Groups related events (e.g., a move = one remove + one add) year int16 forecast year range, no null action object "add" or "remove" agents object "jobs", "households", or "group_quarters" Which agent type to affect agent_expression object no null Pandas query string filtering the agent table location_expression object no null Pandas query string filtering the buildings table amount int16 no null Number of agents to add or remove

agent_expression and location_expression syntax: Both are pandas query strings applied at runtime to the relevant DataFrame. agent_expression filters the agents table (e.g., jobs, households); location_expression filters the buildings table.

Examples from the current data:

action agents agent_expression location_expression amount Meaning add jobs sector_id==6 event_id==9042132 250 Add 250 retail jobs to the event building with id 9042132 add jobs sector_id==3 building_id==8901277 1700 Add 1700 manufacturing jobs to a specific building remove jobs sector_id==9 city_id==501 500 Remove 500 service jobs from buildings in city 501

The event_id column in events_addition is the same as the event_id value used in location_expression — this is how a refiner event targets a planned new building.

Update: Add rows to the employment events CSV for new employment centers or relocations. Add rows to the GQ events CSV for GQ facility changes. Merge both into refiner_events via the build pipeline.

docs.title: landmark_worksites
docs.text:
Major employers whose jobs are protected from simulation randomness. Large factories, university campuses, hospital complexes.

Column Notes building_id Building to protect — receives sp_filter = -1 at startup

docs.title: schools
docs.text:
K-12 school locations and quality scores. Used as HLCM features — school quality affects where families with children choose to live.

Index: bcode (unique)

Column Type Rules Notes bcode int16 unique, no null School building code bname object — School name dcode int32 range [47010–84060], no null School district code gradelist object no null Grade levels served is_grade_school int8 values: 0, 1 1=K-8 point_x float64 no null State plane X coordinate point_y float64 no null State plane Y coordinate totalachievementindex float64 no null School achievement score TOTAL_ENROLLMENT float32 may be null Total enrollment (single value, all grades) zone_id int no null TAZ the school falls in maz_id int no null MAZ the school falls in

Update: Refresh from the Michigan Department of Education database when new schools open, schools close, or achievement scores are updated. For new schools without a score, use the district average.

Common issues: - Coordinates outside the 7-county region — verify data - totalachievementindex = null — causes null neighborhood variables in HLCM; fill with district average

Travel-model enrollment use (TAZ/MAZ zonal inputs, forecast_outputs/travel_model/): this table is the base-year enrollment source. Two limitations are handled downstream and should be understood:

  • Single TOTAL_ENROLLMENT, no grade split. The travel-model pipeline splits it into k-8 vs 9-12 in proportion to the number of grades each school serves (from gradelist). This assumes ~equal enrollment per grade, so it under-weights 9-12 relative to actual grade-level counts (a K-12 school sends 9/13 to k-8, 4/13 to 9-12). Providing measured grades_1_8_enrollment / grades_9_12_enrollment would remove the approximation.
  • dcode is not re-keyed to parcels.school_id. Only ~110 of the 128 population school districts overlap the ~536 dcodes here (≈23% of enrollment sits in non-matching codes). The enrollment step scales base enrollment by a per-district population ratio; districts with no population match carry base enrollment unscaled (scale = 1.0) rather than being dropped. Re-keying dcode to the parcels.school_id coding (25030–82430) would let every district be population-scaled.
  • 321 schools have null TOTAL_ENROLLMENT (counted as 0).

docs.title: Building Construction Costs
docs.text: Construction cost estimates drive the developer model's feasibility analysis (proforma). The model evaluates whether building new structures is financially viable by comparing expected revenue (from real estate price models) against estimated construction costs. If cost exceeds revenue, no new construction occurs in that location.

docs.title: What Is Required
docs.text:
For each developable building type, the model needs a per-square-foot construction cost differentiated by building form, story count, and geographic pricing area. Three pricing areas are defined to reflect local construction market differences across the region.

The developable building types and their general forms are:

Building type IDs General Form 81 Single-family residential 82 Attached condo 83 Multi-family apartment 21, 65 Retail / restaurant 23 Office 31 Manufacturing 32 Wholesale 33 Warehouse 51 Medical office 52 Hospital 53 Residential care 61, 91 Leisure / entertainment 63 Hotel

Building types without a cost mapping (institutional, governmental, agricultural, etc.) are not modeled as developable.

docs.title: Source Data
docs.text: Cost estimates are sourced from a construction cost estimating service, providing per-square-foot costs by building form, story count, and pricing area. The resulting summary table maps each building type to its construction cost per square foot by pricing area.

docs.title: Update Procedure
docs.text:
1. Obtain updated square foot cost estimates for the building forms listed above, for each pricing area.
  2. Map each building form to the corresponding building_type_id codes using the building types lookup file.
  3. Produce a summary cost table and coordinate with the modeling team to incorporate the updated costs into the proforma configuration.

Common issues: - Building types missing from the cost table will have zero construction cost — the model will treat them as infinitely profitable; verify all developable types are covered - Large cost differences between pricing areas should be reviewed for plausibility

docs.title: remi_pce_growth_rate
docs.text:
Annual PCE (Personal Consumption Expenditure) price index growth rate for the region, by forecast year. PCE is a standard measure of economy-wide price change — think of it as the REMI-projected inflation rate for the Southeast Michigan economy. The simulation uses it in exactly one place: cost_shifter_callback in models.py, which inflates new-construction costs forward from the base year before the proforma feasibility calculation. It does not drive property-value appreciation — that's a separate series (remi_pi_growth_rates, personal income, computed per large area) consumed by increase_property_values. An earlier version of this page conflated the two; it doesn't.

Structure: One row per forecast year

Column Type Notes year int16 Forecast year — index pce_growth_rate float64 Annual growth rate as a fraction (e.g., 0.023 = 2.3%); applied cumulatively — each year's cost compounds the previous

A rate of 0.0 means no price change that year. The simulation falls back to a default rate (currently 2.0%) for any year missing from this table, so missing years do not crash the model but will produce incorrect results.

Why region-wide, not per-large-area: REMI's PCE index actually varies by large area (it isn't a true national constant despite being labeled "(Nation)" in the source workbooks). It's deliberately collapsed to one region-wide number here because the base construction-cost table is only differentiated by 3 pricing areas (AA/DET/ROAK), not REMI's 8 large areas — a per-large-area rate would be false precision the cost basis was never built to support.

Produced by: forecast_data_input/development_context/PCE_growth_rate.py. Reads the "PCE-Price Index" row (summary sheet) from each of the 8 large-area SEMCOG Region {horizon} Preliminary Forecast workbooks, log-linear interpolates through the years REMI only reports in 5-year steps (it's annual through 2030, then 5-year jumps), combines the 8 series into one using household-population weights from remi_hh_pop, and converts to year-over-year growth rates. See that script's README.md for the full rationale. This is a different, newer REMI export than the one behind income_growth_rates (Demographics) — they are not regenerated together.

Update: Re-run PCE_growth_rate.py whenever a new REMI preliminary-forecast vintage is delivered (update the 8 workbook paths if the vintage folder name changes), and whenever the forecast horizon extends (e.g., past 2055).

Common issues: - Year range must cover all forecast years; missing years silently fall back to the 2.0% default — verify full coverage - Rates above 5% or below 0% are unusual and should be reviewed against REMI documentation before use - The 8 source workbooks report annual data only through 2030; years beyond that are interpolated, not REMI-native — re-check the interpolation if REMI delivers a fully annual series in a future vintage

docs.title: jobs
docs.text:
Base-year job inventory. One row per job — not per establishment. Every job must be assigned to a building. The primary source is MDOT employment data derived from commercial providers (including Data Axle), geocoded to buildings.

Index: job_id (unique)

Column Type Rules Notes job_id int32 unique, no null building_id int32 join → buildings, no null -1 = unplaced (assigned to pseudo-building at startup) sector_id int8 values: 1–18, no null Employment sector home_based_status int8 values: 0, 1 0=non-home-based, 1=home-based sqft int16 no null Square footage per job

Home-based jobs (value = 1) are located in residential buildings. Non-home-based jobs are in commercial/industrial buildings.

Common issues: - building_id = -1 — unplaced jobs; should be minimal in base year; large unplaced counts indicate geocoding problems - sector_id outside 1–18 — check against SEMCOG sector mapping - building_id referencing non-existent buildings — re-geocode or assign to nearest valid building - Total job count by sector × large area for the base year should match REMI base year employment

docs.title: How the model uses key job columns
docs.text:
Column Used by (model step) How it's used / why it matters building_id (-1 = unplaced) ELCM -1 flags a job the ELCM must place this year; already-placed jobs stay put (job relocation is currently off). New jobs added by jobs_transition start at -1. sector_id ELCM segmentation A separate ELCM is run per sector (× home-based status); the sector also drives sector-specific job-accessibility variables. home_based_status ELCM Home-based jobs (1) sit in residential buildings and are not placed by the building-level ELCM; non-home-based (0) compete for vacant_job_spaces. sqft / building_sqft_per_job building job capacity Converts non-residential floor space into job_spaces (see buildings) — the supply that non-home-based jobs fill.

base_job_space is a separate, derived table — a frozen base-year snapshot of each building's non-home-based job count, used for indicators and trend variables. It is not the live job capacity (that is job_spaces, recomputed from current non_residential_sqft).

docs.title: annual_employment_control_totals
docs.text:
Target job counts by large area × sector × home-based status × year. The jobs_transition model step uses this to add or remove jobs annually.

Index: Multi-index (year, sector_id, home_based_status) Generated by: A forecast controls pipeline that converts REMI employment exports to SEMCOG 18-sector classifications.

Column Type Allowed Values Notes year int16 all forecast years Part of multi-index sector_id int8 1–18 Part of multi-index home_based_status int8 0, 1 Part of multi-index large_area_id int16 8 valid codes total_number_of_jobs int32 no null Target job count

Sample rows (year 2021, Detroit / large_area_id=161, non-home-based, varied sectors):

year sector_id home_based_status large_area_id total_number_of_jobs 2021 1 0 161 221 2021 3 0 161 13,035 2021 6 0 161 3,982 2021 10 0 161 19,133 2021 13 0 161 51,581

Important: All combinations of year × sector × large area × home-based status must be present for all forecast years. Missing cells cause the transition model to skip that segment entirely — jobs in that segment will neither grow nor shrink.

REMI-to-SEMCOG sector mapping: REMI uses its own sector classification, which differs from the SEMCOG 18-sector scheme. A crosswalk file maps REMI sectors to SEMCOG sectors. This crosswalk must be applied before generating control totals.

Common issues: - Missing sector/year combinations — model will not grow/shrink those jobs; check that all 18 sectors × 8 large areas × 2 home-based statuses × all years are present - Base year total jobs across all sectors should approximately match the row count in jobs

docs.title: employed_workers_rate
docs.text:
The fraction of the population in each age group that is employed, by large area and year.

How it's used: Each simulation year, after households transition, the workers_adjustment_model step compares the simulated household population (by age group × large area) against the employment target from this table. It adjusts each household's workers count to match the REMI employment target, ensuring the simulated workforce stays aligned with regional economic projections.

Index: large_area_id

Column Type Notes large_area_id int16 8 valid large area codes — row index Age_Group object Age group label (e.g., "Ages 16-19") age_min int8 Lower bound of age group age_max float Upper bound of age group (NaN for the open-ended oldest group) one column per year float64 Employed worker rate for that age group × large area × year (values in [0, 1])

Structure: 104 rows (8 large areas × 13 age groups), with year columns running from the historical reference period through the end of the forecast horizon.

Age groups: 16–19, 20–21, 22–24, 25–29, 30–34, 35–44, 45–54, 55–59, 60–61, 62–64, 65–69, 70–74, 75+.

Sample rows — Ages 25-29 across all large areas, showing regional variation:

large_area_id Age_Group age_min age_max 2020 2025 2030 2040 2050 3 (Wayne excl. Detroit) Ages 25-29 25 29 0.724 0.753 0.758 0.758 0.756 5 (City of Detroit) Ages 25-29 25 29 0.680 0.737 0.740 0.744 0.751 93 (Livingston) Ages 25-29 25 29 0.779 0.822 0.821 0.820 0.818 99 (Macomb) Ages 25-29 25 29 0.753 0.802 0.808 0.806 0.805 115 (Monroe) Ages 25-29 25 29 0.748 0.788 0.797 0.803 0.799 125 (Oakland) Ages 25-29 25 29 0.771 0.813 0.812 0.811 0.810 147 (St. Clair) Ages 25-29 25 29 0.726 0.766 0.775 0.782 0.775 161 (Washtenaw) Ages 25-29 25 29 0.754 0.803 0.804 0.803 0.802

Note: This is not the same as the labor force participation rate in the REMI forecast. REMI's labor force participation rate measures the share of the population that is working or actively seeking work. employed_workers_rate measures the share that is actually employed, derived by dividing projected employment by projected population for each age group × large area. The two rates differ because labor force participation includes unemployed job-seekers.

Update: Derive from REMI employment forecasts by large area, age group, and year. Divide projected employment by projected population in each age group × large area. Update when new REMI runs are available.

Common issues: - All 8 large areas and all 13 age groups must be present (104 rows total) - Year columns must cover the full simulation range - Values outside [0, 1] indicate a data error

This domain covers geographic reference tables that define the spatial hierarchy used throughout the model. These tables are used for aggregation, joining, and assigning spatial identifiers to parcels, buildings, households, and jobs.

docs.title: zones
docs.text:
Traffic Analysis Zones used for travel demand modeling. Parcels reference zone_id, and travel data is indexed by zone pairs.

Index: zone_id (unique)

Column Type Rules Notes zone_id int16 range [1 – 2811], no null Model TAZ identifier taz object no null Full TAZ GEOID string tazce10_n int32 no null Census TAZ code (used for joining with travel model) acres float64 no null Zone area in acres

Note: TransCAD uses tazce10_n codes internally. When converting travel matrices from OMX, always map through this table to translate travel model TAZ codes to zone_id. Using raw travel model codes will silently produce incorrect accessibility measurements.

Common issues: - Any parcel without a matching zone_id in this table will have null travel-based variables — verify full TAZ coverage for the region

docs.title: semmcds
docs.text:
Municipal entity reference table — cities, townships, villages in the 7-county region.

Index: semmcd_id (unique)

Column Type Rules Notes semmcd_id int16 range [5 – 7100], no null SEMCOG MCD code — this is the authoritative municipal identifier county_id int16 — Parent county large_area_id int16 — Parent large area area_name object no null Municipality name

semmcd vs city_id: Throughout the model, semmcd is the official municipal code. The column name city_id appears in many tables as a synonym for semmcd — except in the City of Detroit, where city_id refers to a neighborhood subdivision rather than the municipality as a whole. This is a legacy naming convention. When working with Detroit data, verify whether a city_id value represents the whole city (Detroit's semmcd is 5) or a neighborhood code. See the Glossary for full context.

docs.title: counties
docs.text:
The 7 SE Michigan counties. This is a constant table — it rarely needs updating.

Index: county_id (unique)

Valid county codes (Michigan county FIPS codes):

Code County 93 Livingston 99 Macomb 115 Monroe 125 Oakland 147 St. Clair 161 Washtenaw 163 Wayne Column Type Rules county_id int16 7 valid codes, no null county_name object no null

docs.title: large_areas
docs.text:
The 8 modeling zones used for model segmentation, control totals, and output aggregation. This is a constant table — it does not change between forecast cycles.

Index: large_area_id (unique)

Valid large area codes:

Code Area Note 3 Wayne County (excl. Detroit) Custom code — splits Wayne County 5 City of Detroit Custom code — splits Detroit from rest of Wayne 93 Livingston County Michigan FIPS code 99 Macomb County Michigan FIPS code 115 Monroe County Michigan FIPS code 125 Oakland County Michigan FIPS code 147 St. Clair County Michigan FIPS code 161 Washtenaw County Michigan FIPS code

Wayne County (FIPS 163) is split into two large areas — the City of Detroit (code 5) and the rest of Wayne County (code 3). All other large areas share their code with the Michigan county FIPS number. The counties table uses FIPS code 163 for all of Wayne County; the split into codes 3 and 5 only exists in large_areas.

Column Type Notes large_area_id int16 8 valid codes, no null large_area_name object Internal short name (e.g., "outway", "det", "oak") — use large_area_id for joins large_area_group_id int8 Values 1–4: regional grouping — 1=Suburban Tri-County (Wayne suburbs, Oakland, Macomb), 2=Western Corridor (Washtenaw, Livingston), 3=Outer Counties (Monroe, St. Clair), 4=Detroit alt_large_id int8 Values 1–8: sequential alias for the 8 large areas, used in some model output routines

docs.title: micro_zones
docs.text:
Model input (anchor geography). micro_zones is the MAZ→TAZ crosswalk used throughout the model. Parcels and buildings carry a maz_id, and their TAZ (zone_id) is derived from MAZ through this table's 1:1 maz_id → zone_id mapping. The model uses MAZ to anchor building locations (esp. on parcels that cross boundaries) and to assign new buildings to fine-grained zones.

Micro Analysis Zones (MAZ) are sub-units of TAZs used in activity-based travel demand modeling. Each TAZ is divided into approximately 10 MAZs on average.

~28,647 MAZs across the region, each nested within a TAZ. Source: creator.terminus_maz_v3 (PostGIS, EPSG:2898). The HDF table key is micro_zones.

Index: maz_id

Column Type Notes maz_id int Unique MAZ identifier (index; from maz_seqid) zone_id int Parent TAZ — joins to zones.zone_id (the MAZ→TAZ crosswalk) tazce10_n int Census TAZ code — joins to zones.tazce10_n acres float MAZ area in acres

Relationship to other geography tables:

TAZ (zones)
  └── MAZ (micro_zones, ~10 per TAZ on average → 28,647 total)
        ├── parcels.maz_id  → micro_zones.maz_id ; parcels.zone_id derived via micro_zones.zone_id
        └── buildings → building_to_maz_override (straddling buildings) else parcel-inherited

Parcels now carry both maz_id and zone_id columns (assigned by spatially joining parcel centroids to the MAZ boundary layer). This replaces the earlier approach where MAZ was derived only at output time.

Update: Regenerate when the MAZ delineation changes. Coordinate with the travel demand modeling team, as MAZ boundaries must align with the TAZ structure used in the travel model.

docs.title: building_to_maz_override
docs.text:
Base-year building→MAZ/TAZ override. Present in the base-year HDF (~23,870 rows). For buildings whose parcel straddles a MAZ/TAZ boundary, this table overrides the default parcel-inherited MAZ/TAZ, assigning the building its own maz_id (and derived zone_id) based on actual building location. Loaded and used by the model.

Index: building_id

Column Type Notes maz_id int Overriding MAZ for this building (joins micro_zones.maz_id) zone_id int Overriding TAZ, derived from the MAZ via micro_zones.zone_id

docs.title: parcel_maz_crossing_shares
docs.text:
New-construction MAZ allocation weights. Specifies, for each parcel that straddles a MAZ boundary, the land area fraction in each MAZ. Used to assign new buildings on crossing parcels: each new building draws one MAZ probabilistically, weighted by these area shares. ~41k rows (crossing parcels only); non-crossing parcels are implicit (single dominant MAZ).

Columns:

Column Type Notes parcel_id int Parcel identifier (index) maz_id int One of the MAZs this parcel crosses (joins micro_zones.maz_id) area_sqft float Land area of parcel within this MAZ (square feet) share float Fraction of parcel's total area in this MAZ; sums to 1.0 per parcel_id taz_id int Parent TAZ of this MAZ portion

Data note: Presence in this table is the indicator that a parcel crosses a MAZ boundary. Parcels not in this table are non-crossing (single dominant MAZ from their centroid).

docs.title: Update Notes
docs.text:
zones and semmcds — update when TAZ or MCD boundaries change (typically when census boundaries are updated or new municipalities form or dissolve).

counties and large_areas — stable definitions tied to the 7-county region and 8 modeling zones. Only update if the model's geographic scope changes, which is a major structural decision.

When updating any geography table, verify all downstream joins: - parcels.zone_id → zones - parcels.maz_id → micro_zones - parcels.semmcd → semmcds - parcels.county_id → counties - parcels.large_area_id → large_areas - building_to_maz_override.maz_id → micro_zones (and .zone_id → zones)

Missing join matches will result in null spatial attributes on parcels, which propagates to all buildings, households, and jobs on those parcels.

Primary source: PostgreSQL parcel and building database

This domain covers the spatial foundation of the model — every parcel, every building, the zoning overlay, and land use and building type definitions.

docs.title: parcels
docs.text:
The foundational spatial table. Every building must have a parcel_id that exists here. Used for all spatial joins in the model.

Index: parcel_id (unique)

Columns:

Column Type Rules Notes parcel_id int32 unique, no null Primary key census_bg_id int32 no null Census block group GEOID centroid_x float64 no null State plane X coordinate (Michigan GeoRef / NAD83) centroid_y float64 no null State plane Y coordinate city_id int16 no null Municipality code (= semmcd outside Detroit; neighborhood id inside Detroit — see Glossary) county_id int16 7 valid county codes Must be one of the 7 SE Michigan counties land_use_type_id int16 join → land_use_types Must reference a valid land use type large_area_id int16 8 valid codes One of the 8 modeling zones parcel_sqft int32 no null Parcel area in sq ft pptytax float64 no null Property tax millage rate school_id int32 no null School district reference semmcd int16 no null SEMCOG MCD code sev_value int32 no null State Equalized Value landvalue int32 no null Assessed land value bldgimprval int32 no null Total building improvement value for the parcel (all buildings combined); used to compute buildings.improvement_value and the bldg_impr_land_ratio feature in the developer model zone_id int16 no null TAZ zone reference

Common issues: - Parcels with zone_id = null after join — no TAZ match; check that the parcel's zone code exists in the TAZ boundary table - large_area_id outside the 8 allowed values — usually out-of-region parcels; filter them out - Coordinate outliers — verify projection (Michigan GeoRef state plane) and check for misplaced records

docs.title: How the model uses key parcel columns
docs.text: Column Used by (model step) How it's used / why it matters landvalue developer, demolition Assessed land value. Paired with building improvement value as the land-to-improvement ratio — a high ratio signals teardown pressure in the demolition model — and land value feeds developer feasibility. bldgimprval developer, demolition Total building improvement value on the parcel. Allocated to each building as improvement_value; the land-to-improvement ratio built from it feeds the demolition-risk score.

docs.title: buildings
docs.text: Every residential unit and job must be assigned to a building. This is the most-used table in the simulation. Building count is close to parcel count — most parcels have one building.

docs.title: Base-year building snapshot and event cutoff
docs.text:
The buildings table is an assembled base-year inventory, not a direct copy of the source building view. For each forecast cycle, the input build:

  1. loads the building GIS view for the year immediately before the base year;
  2. removes all scheduled deletion events dated in the base year;
  3. adds all scheduled addition events dated in the base year; and
  4. validates the resulting buildings against parcels and building types.

For the current cycle, this means the 2024 building view is advanced to the 2025 base-year snapshot. Deletions are applied before additions. The source building view and the complete set of base-year additions and deletions are therefore the data-development inputs that determine whether the base-year buildings table is complete.

Index: building_id (unique)

Columns exported to model input:

Column Type Rules Notes building_id int32 unique, no null Primary key parcel_id int32 join → parcels, no null Every building must have a valid parcel building_type_id int8 join → building_types, no null See building type codes below year_built int16 range [1760 – base year], no null Cap at base year residential_units int16 no null 0 for non-residential non_residential_sqft int64 no null 0 for residential sqft_per_unit int16 no null 0 for non-residential stories float64 no null improvement_value float64 no null Derived during assembly: parcel's bldgimprval allocated to each building proportionally by its share of total building sqft on the parcel land_area int32 no null Building footprint market_value float64 — Total assessed value

city_id is not a required base-year buildings input field. Municipal geography is owned by parcels.city_id; do not maintain a separate building-level city assignment. Likewise, maz_id is established from the parcel MAZ, with exceptions supplied through building_to_maz_override in the Geography domain.

Building type codes:

ID Range General Type 11, 13, 14 Institutional 21 Retail 23 Office 31, 32, 33 Industrial 41, 42 TCU 51, 52, 53 Medical 61, 63, 91 Entertainment 65 Hospitality 71 Other 81, 82, 83, 84 Residential 92, 93 Institutional (education) 94 Other commercial 95 TCU

Common issues: - parcel_id not found in parcels — orphaned buildings; these break the spatial join chain - year_built after base year — cap to base year - Buildings with both residential_units > 0 AND non_residential_sqft > 0 — mixed-use is valid; verify intentional - residential_units > 0 but sqft_per_unit = 0 — the model uses sqft_per_unit for feasibility analysis; assign a reasonable default

docs.title: How the model uses key building columns
docs.text:
Beyond being descriptive attributes, several building columns directly drive model steps. Some values are derived at runtime from the input columns above (marked derived) — listed here so you can see why the inputs matter.

Column Used by (model step) How it's used / why it matters non_residential_sqft → job_spaces (derived) ELCM (employment location choice) Job capacity = non_residential_sqft ÷ building_sqft_per_job (by building type). The ELCM fills only vacant_job_spaces (capacity − jobs present, floored at 0) — the supply ceiling for employment. Understate the sqft and jobs can't locate there; overstate it and the building over-absorbs jobs. residential_units → vacant_residential_units (derived) HLCM (household location choice) Household capacity. Households are placed only into vacant units; residential_units = 0 means no household can live there. market_value REPM (price model) Seeds the base-year sqft_price_res / sqft_price_nonres and is a static base-year anchor / predictor in the hedonic price model (it is not rewritten during the run). sqft_price_res / sqft_price_nonres (derived) REPM → developer, HLCM/ELCM The model's working prices. REPM re-predicts them each year; the developer reads nearby values to judge feasibility, and location-choice models score them. improvement_value demolition model Improvement value per sqft and the land-to-improvement ratio feed the building's demolition-risk score. sp_filter demolition, relocation, location choice Special-building marker. Negative = protected/excluded: update_sp_filter sets -1 for institutional types (schools, hospitals, government, libraries, religious/civic) so they are never demolished or re-chosen; pseudo-buildings are -2.

docs.title: zoning
docs.text:
Controls what can be built on each parcel. Directly drives the developer/feasibility model.

Index: parcel_id (unique)

Columns:

Column Type Rules Notes parcel_id int32 join → parcels, no null future_use object no null Future land use designation max_dua float64 range [0 – 126], no null Max dwelling units per acre max_far float64 no null Max floor area ratio max_height int16 no null Max building height (ft) max_stories float16 range [1 – 73], no null Max number of stories pct_undev float64 range [0 – 100], no null Percent of parcel undeveloped is_developable int — 0=not developable, 1=developable, 2=developable with Underground Storage Tank (UST) present. Value 2 parcels are treated as developable but have 10 percentage points added to pct_undev, making them slightly less competitive for new development. type81 – type95 int — 1 = building type allowed on this parcel

Common issues: - pct_undev = null — treated as 0% developable in the model; fill with 0 or actual value - Missing is_developable — defaults to not developable; verify coverage - Any parcel in zoning must have a matching parcel_id in parcels

docs.title: How the model uses key zoning columns
docs.text:
The entire zoning table exists to constrain the developer / feasibility model — it decides where and what new construction is allowed.

Column Used by (model step) How it's used / why it matters is_developable feasibility Gate: 0 = never built on. 2 (UST present) is still developable but adds 10 points to pct_undev, making the parcel slightly less competitive. pct_undev developer Share of the parcel treated as available for new construction — scales how much can be built. max_dua / max_far / max_height / max_stories developer pro-forma Hard caps; the feasibility check discards any building proposal that exceeds them. type81 – type95 developer Which building types are allowed on the parcel; feasibility only considers allowed forms.

docs.title: land_use_types
docs.text:

docs.title: Street Networks
docs.text:
Primary source: OpenStreetMap (walk network), SEMCOG highway/TDM network (drive network) File: semcog_networks.h5 — a separate HDF5 from the main model input file

The street network file provides the road and path geometry used by Pandana to compute dynamic neighborhood accessibility variables during the simulation. Each year, the build_networks_2050 step loads these networks, snaps parcels and buildings to the nearest node, and aggregates nearby jobs, households, and amenities into building-level variables used by the location choice models.

This file is distinct from the pre-computed accessibility indicators — those are static parcel-level outputs. The network file enables the simulation to recompute dynamic, year-varying accessibility each year as the distribution of jobs and households shifts.

docs.title: File Structure
docs.text:
The HDF5 contains one set of tables per named network. Each network has:

Table type Purpose nodes_* Network node locations (x, y coordinates + node ID) edges_* Connections between nodes with travel cost attributes local_nodes_* Subset of nodes for neighborhood-level queries (drive networks only) local_edges_* Corresponding subset of edges (drive networks only)

docs.title: Networks in the File

docs.title: Walk — osm_walk_2024
docs.text:
OpenStreetMap road and path data, 2024 vintage. Replaced osm_roads_walk_2020 in Jul 2026 and has 32% more edges, so walk-based neighborhood variables shift — compare against a previous run before relying on them.

Cost used for queries: feet (distance) or minutes (time, at 3 mph) Typical query radius: 500 m (neighborhood density), 1,500 m (local population/jobs)

feet = meters × 3.280839895.

docs.title: Drive — highway_ext_2020
docs.text:
SEMCOG highway / TDM road network, built from highway_ext_2020_UPDATED.shp.

Table Columns nodes_highway_ext_2020 x, y, nodeid edges_highway_ext_2020 from, to, peak_mins, nonpk_mins, miles nodes_highway_ext_2020_local x, y, nodeid edges_highway_ext_2020_local from, to, peak_mins, nonpk_mins, miles

Cost used for queries: peak_mins (commute accessibility) or nonpk_mins (off-peak) Typical query radius: 15–60 minutes (job access, retail proximity)

docs.title: Bike — osm_bike_2024, osm_bike_comfort_2024
docs.text:
Included for future use; no model component reads them yet.

osm_bike_2024 carries real distance at a 10 mph basis. osm_bike_comfort_2024 is the bicycle level-of-traffic-stress network — minutes_w1 and minutes_w2 are both stress-penalised times, not clock times, so feet_weighted (derived from minutes_w2) is a stress-weighted distance rather than measurable feet. Use osm_bike_2024 when real distance is needed.

docs.title: Retired
docs.text:
• highway_ext_2030 — dropped Jul 2026. It was largely the same as the 2020 network, 2030 is near, and there is no updated 2030 build to pair with the updated 2020 one. All years now use highway_ext_2020. (The separate travel_data_2030 travel-time skims are unaffected — different data.)
  • osm_roads_walk_2020 — replaced by osm_walk_2024.

docs.title: What the Networks Compute
docs.text:
Each simulation year, Pandana uses these networks to produce node-level aggregations. These are then broadcast to buildings and parcels. Key variables computed:

Walk-based (neighborhood density): - Residential and non-residential density within 500 m - Population and households within 1,500 m - Income mix, household demographics within 1,500 m - Retail and service job counts within 500–2,000 m - Average residential and non-residential prices nearby - Transit stops within quarter mile

Drive-based (regional access): - Jobs within 30, 45, and 60 minutes - Population within 10 and 20 minutes - Retail and shopping jobs within 15 and 30 minutes - Nearby school achievement scores

docs.title: How Parcels Connect to the Network
docs.text:
Each parcel has a nodeid_walk and nodeid_drv column — the ID of the nearest walk or drive network node. These are pre-computed and stored in the parcels table. Buildings inherit them via the parcel. These columns are generated during model setup and do not need to be manually prepared.

If a parcel's node ID is missing or invalid, that building will have null network-based variables, which can affect location choice model predictions.

docs.title: Update Procedure
docs.text:
semcog_networks.h5 is assembled by forecast_data_input/accessibility/build_semcog_networks.py, which pulls from the network builds produced for the accessibility analysis:

Network in this file Comes from highway_ext_2020 (+ _local) network_highway_2024_aug2025.h5 osm_walk_2024, osm_bike_2024, osm_bike_comfort_2024 network_walkbike_2024_aug2025.h5

Those source files also contain other tables (including an older, superseded copy of the highway network inside the walkbike file), so take each network from the source listed above rather than by table name alone.

The network file should be regenerated when: - Road network geometry changes significantly (new highways, removed roads) - A new forecast cycle uses a different base year - Walk network coverage needs updating (OSM data vintage)

Walk network update: 1. Download updated OSM data for SE Michigan 2. Process into Pandana-compatible nodes/edges (feet, minutes, meters cost columns) 3. Snap parcel centroids to nearest walk node → update parcels.nodeid_walk 4. Write new tables into semcog_networks.h5

Drive network update: 1. Export node/edge tables from the SEMCOG TDM (TransCAD) network 2. Ensure cost columns are peak_mins, nonpk_mins, miles 3. Generate "local" subsets (nodes/edges within the 7-county region) 4. Snap parcel centroids to nearest drive node → update parcels.nodeid_drv 5. Write new tables into semcog_networks.h5 6. Update the network configuration file if table names change

After updating the network file: - Verify nodeid_walk and nodeid_drv coverage in parcels — count nulls and parcels with no node match - Run a test simulation year and check that neighborhood variables are non-null for most buildings - If node IDs change, the parcel columns must be recomputed — new node IDs won't match old parcel assignments

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text:
• Parcels not snapping to network — parcel coordinates outside the network coverage area; check for projection mismatches (all data should be in Michigan state plane)
  • Missing local edges — the local network subset must fully cover the 7-county region; edges that cross county boundaries may be clipped
  • Expecting a 2030 network — it was retired in Jul 2026; all years use highway_ext_2020. If planned improvements need representing again, restore both the HDF tables and the available_networks_2050.yaml entry, and reinstate the year-based branch in models.py

docs.title: Travel Data
docs.text:
Primary source: SEMCOG travel demand model outputs (OMX matrix files → CSV)

Travel data provides zone-to-zone travel times and mode choice logsums used as features in the HLCM and ELCM to capture commute accessibility and transit competitiveness.

docs.title: Tables in This Domain
docs.text: Table Description Source travel_data Base-year zone-to-zone travel skims CSV (converted from OMX) travel_data_2030 Future-year zone-to-zone travel skims CSV (converted from OMX)

docs.title: Source OMX Files
docs.text:
The travel demand model produces zone-to-zone skim matrices in OMX format. These must be converted to flat CSV before inclusion in the model input file.

Typical skim files include: - Auto travel time (AM peak and midday) - Transit travel time (AM peak and midday) - Home-based work logsums by income group (low/mid/high) - Home-based other (non-work) logsum

docs.title: travel_data
docs.text:
Base-year zone-to-zone travel skims. One row per origin-destination pair.

Index: Multi-index (from_zone_id, to_zone_id) (unique pairs) All columns cast to float32 in the build pipeline

Columns:

Column Type Rules Notes from_zone_id int16 range [1 – max zone], no null Origin TAZ (model zone_id) to_zone_id int16 range [1 – max zone], no null Destination TAZ am_auto_total_time float32 no null AM peak auto travel time (minutes) am_transit_total_time float32 no null AM peak transit total time (minutes) am_work_lowinc_logsum float32 no null AM work trip mode choice logsum, low income am_work_midinc_logsum float32 no null AM work trip mode choice logsum, mid income am_work_highinc_logsum float32 no null AM work trip mode choice logsum, high income midday_auto_total_time float32 no null Midday auto travel time (minutes) midday_transit_total_time float32 no null Midday transit total time midday_other_logsum float32 no null Midday non-work trip mode choice logsum

What is a mode choice logsum? The mode choice logsum is the expected maximum utility a traveler can achieve between an origin-destination pair, considering all available travel modes (auto, transit, walk, etc.) and their relative costs and times. A higher logsum value means better overall multimodal accessibility between two zones — not just faster driving, but better access by any mode.

These logsums are not destination choice logsums (which aggregate over all destinations). They are zone-to-zone matrices used in UrbanSim as gravity-type impedance weights: the model computes zone-level accessibility as Σ [population or jobs at destination] × exp(logsum) across all destination zones, capturing how well each zone is connected to opportunities by all modes combined. Work-trip logsums are segmented by income because lower-income households are more sensitive to transit access and cost.

docs.title: travel_data_2030
docs.text: Future-year travel skims representing conditions after planned transportation investments. Same schema as travel_data. Allows the model to use time-varying travel conditions for later simulation years.

docs.title: TAZ ID Mapping — Critical
docs.text:
The travel demand model uses its own internal TAZ codes, which differ from the model's zone_id values. Always map through the zones table when converting OMX to CSV:

Travel model TAZ code  →  zones.tazce10_n  →  zones.zone_id

Using the wrong TAZ codes will silently produce incorrect accessibility measurements without any error — this is one of the most common and hard-to-detect mistakes in this pipeline.

docs.title: Conversion from OMX to CSV
docs.text: General process: 1. Open OMX files using the openmatrix or omx Python library 2. Extract each skim as a zone × zone matrix 3. Flatten to long format: one row per origin-destination pair, one column per skim 4. Map travel model TAZ codes to zone_id via the zones table 5. Join all skims on (from_zone_id, to_zone_id) to produce one combined CSV 6. Save with the multi-index (from_zone_id, to_zone_id)

docs.title: Update Checklist (New Forecast Cycle)
docs.text:
• [ ] Get new OMX skims from the travel model run (base year and future year)
  • [ ] Run OMX-to-CSV conversion
  • [ ] Verify TAZ ID mapping — travel model codes → zones.tazce10_n → zones.zone_id
  • [ ] Verify TAZ coverage — all zones should appear as both origin and destination
  • [ ] Verify no null values in any skim column
  • [ ] Check plausibility: auto times must be positive; near-zero values are expected only for intra-zonal pairs
  • [ ] Confirm row count = number of zones² (all origin-destination combinations present)

Common issues: - TAZ ID mismatch — always map through the zones table; see note above - Zero or negative travel times — usually an OMX extraction error; auto times must be positive - Missing zone pairs — fill with a high default time (e.g., 999 minutes) rather than leaving null
